newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African Afrikaans media gains rising ad spending.
newsitem.headline: S.African Afrikaans media gains rising ad spending.

text.p: Long dominated by English-speaking interests, South Africa's media is in flux and newspapers who cater for Afrikaans speakers may be the winners.

The language, developed in South Africa over the last 340 years by descendents of Dutch settlers, is now one of the most widely spoken in the country and advertisers are flocking to support Afrikaans publications.

This is knocking the traditional supremacy of the English press for six, allowing Afrikaans publishing house Nasionale Pers Bpk (Naspers) to crow in its latest annual report on Tuesday that its titles were now seen as "winning newspapers" by advertisers.
"In contrast, some of the leading English dailies are ranked as 'losing newspapers'," the group said.
The group is particularly proud of the fact that its Cape Town flagship, Die Burger, had overtaken the Independent Group's Cape Argus as the market leader in the Western Cape.

Analysts attribute this shift to the decision by the South African Broadcasting Corporation to cutback on broadcasts in Afrikaans. Many Afrikaans speakers have switched off and are returning to reading newspapers.
Business magazine Finance Week reported that, in line with the international trend, circulation growth for most South African newspapers was stagnant.
But Audit Bureau of Circulation figures between 1992 and 1996 showed that the circulaton growth of English dailies had shrunk 11 percent while that of Afrikaans dailies had grown by 18 percent.
"Adspend should therefore increasingly be following the Afrikaans papers, which seems to have been confirmed in latest full-year results from Naspers," Finance Week said.

To hedge its bets, Naspers has also been making inroads into the growing black market through City Press. It recently sold 51 percent of the newspaper to black empowerment groups while retaining management control.
"Advertisers are realising more and more that City Press offers a unique channel to black consumers," the Naspers annual report said.
The group is also moving into regional newspapers and radio stations.

Finance Week said that the English press had also not been helped by the growing fragmentation of the market as more local titles were launched and overseas magazines and newspapers moved into South Africa.

English newspapers still pull in the bulk of advertising revenue, but steady growth and a focus on niche markets are boosting Naspers' fortunes, allowing chairman Ton Vosloo to sound positively bullish about future prospects in his annual review.
"Our five-year estimates show that Naspers' earnings can achieve strong real growth," he said.
